a: Look among the nations
t: Nations, scoffers or traitors?
p: The Hebrew has "among the nations"; the Greek and the Qumran commentary have a word for people.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 has the other words of the verse but this word is restored, not preserved, in its printout
readings.plain: Look among the nations

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text); quoted in Acts 13:41
readings.plain: Look, you scoffers

readings.w: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab), as published by Horgan and in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible; this site's transcription data does not include this scroll
readings.plain: Look, you traitors

why: The Hebrew is the base text, and "among the nations" fits the verse: God's act is for all to see. The Greek and the commentary both read a word for people, not a place.
b: The Greek "scoffers" is probably a translation of the Hebrew bogedim ("traitors"), the reading the Qumran commentary has, since the same letters can be misread as bagoyim ("among the nations"). If so, the Greek Acts 13:41 quotes does not preserve a separate Hebrew text but a reading. The Greek also adds "and vanish" after "be astonished." Acts follows the Greek; the Plain of Acts is given in the note.

a: the Chaldeans
t: Chaldeans, or Kittim?
p: The Dead Sea commentary, as published, quotes "Chaldeans" and then says they mean the Kittim; Duhm proposed changing the text.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves "the Chaldeans" and "and hasty" in its printout
readings.plain: the Chaldeans

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: the Chaldeans

readings.w: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab), as published: the quotation has Chaldeans, and the comment says they are the Kittim (an interpretation, not a different text); this site's transcription data does not include this scroll
readings.plain: the Kittim (in the comment)

readings.w: Bernhard Duhm's emendation (1906), a proposal, not a witness
readings.plain: the Kittim

why: Every Hebrew and Greek witness read in this site's data has "Chaldeans," and the portrait fits Babylon (see the note on when the book was written). The Kittim are the pesher's reading of the people, not its text.

a: the wolves of evening
t: Wolves of the evening or of Arabia?
p: A one-letter question: the Hebrew 'erev is "evening", while 'arav would be "Arabia" or "desert."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 (the words are restored in its printout, so it gives no help)
readings.plain: the wolves of evening

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: the wolves of Arabia

why: "Evening" is the Hebrew text, and wolves hunt at dusk (Zephaniah 3:3 has "wolves of the evening"). The Greek reads the same letters as the name of the desert.

a: Their faces are set straight ahead
t: Where do their faces point?
p: The Hebrew word is unique; it can mean "forward," "east," or "east wind."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves megammat but restores qadimah and panehem in its printout
readings.en: the thrust of their faces forward (or eastward)
readings.plain: Their faces are set straight ahead

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome)
readings.plain: Their faces are a burning wind

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: They stand face to face against them

why: Megammat occurs only here. Qadimah means "east" or "forward" (it is the front of space as well as the sunrise). "Forward" suits an army coming from Babylon to the west, where "east" does not.
b: The Vulgate takes qadimah as qadim, the scorching east wind. If that is right, the nation comes like a desert wind (1:11 also has "wind"). The Greek reads the word as a military posture.

a: Then it sweeps on like the wind and moves past
t: Wind, or a change of spirit?
p: The Greek says the nation changes its mind and makes atonement; the Hebrew does not. Goes with the next line.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 has "then" and "passed on" but restores "wind"
readings.en: then the wind passed on and crossed over, and he is guilty
readings.plain: Then it sweeps on like the wind and moves past

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.orig: τότε μεταβαλεῖ τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ διελεύσεται καὶ ἐξιλάσεται
readings.en: then he will change his spirit, and pass through, and make atonement
readings.plain: Then he changes his spirit, passes through, and makes atonement

why: The Hebrew is the older base and makes sense. The Greek reads 'asham ("guilty") as a verb, "make amends," and zu ("this") with the next clause.

a: a guilty one, whose own strength is his god
t: "His strength is his god" or "this strength is for my God"?
p: The Greek ends the verse with a different thought. Goes with the line before.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 reads the word "this" in the printout
readings.en: this his strength [is] to his god
readings.plain: a guilty one, whose own strength is his god

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.orig: αὕτη ἡ ἰσχὺς τῷ θεῷ μου
readings.en: this strength is for my God
readings.plain: this strength belongs to my God

why: The Hebrew accuses the nation of idolizing its strength, which fits 1:16. The Greek puts it in the prophet's mouth as praise of God.

a: we will not die
t: "We will not die" or "you do not die"?
p: A rabbinic tradition says the scribes changed "you" to "we" to avoid saying that God might die.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); the Greek and the Latin Vulgate agree with it; Mur88's words are restored in the printout, so it gives no help
readings.plain: we will not die

readings.w: A rabbinic tradition (the Mekhilta of Rabbi Ishmael and other midrashim), which lists this verse among the "corrections of the scribes" (tiqqune soferim); no manuscript is known to have it
readings.plain: you do not die

why: Every witness I could read has "we." The rabbinic claim is that the text once said "you," and that the scribes softened it; the claim is an ancient tradition about an earlier text, not a manuscript.
b: Carmel McCarthy's study of the corrections argues that the lists are late and not always consistent, and that some entries describe a rabbinic exegetical idea, not a change in the text. If "you do not die" was ever the text, the line would be God's undying nature, set against the mortal Judah; as it stands it is the prophet's confidence that Israel will not perish.

a: Will he, then, go on emptying his net
t: Emptying the net, or casting it?
p: The Greek says "he will cast his net"; the Hebrew says "empty."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (no scroll preserves the verse in the printout)
readings.en: will he then empty his net
readings.plain: Will he, then, go on emptying his net

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.orig: διὰ τοῦτο ἀμφιβαλεῖ τὸ ἀμφίβληστρον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: therefore he will cast his net
readings.plain: Because of this he will keep casting his net

why: The Hebrew verb "empty" fits the fisher's net being emptied of the catch to be filled again. The Greek reads it as a statement, not a question.

a: take my place on the tower
t: Tower or rock?
p: The Hebrew has a siege-work or rampart; the Greek has a rock.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); the words are restored or absent in the printout
readings.plain: take my place on the tower

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.en: I will go up on a rock
readings.plain: go up on the rock

why: Matsor means a fortified place, and the first line ("my post") already has a watching image. The Greek petran reads tsur ("rock") for it.

a: It gasps toward the end, and it will not lie
t: Does the vision pant, or rise?
p: The Greek has the vision "rise" at the end.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves vayafeach ("it pants") and "does not lie" but restores "for the appointed time" and laqets ("toward the end"); 4Q82 does not preserve the verse
readings.en: and it pants toward the end, and does not lie
readings.plain: It gasps toward the end, and it will not lie

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.orig: ἀνατελεῖ εἰς πέρας καὶ οὐκ εἰς κενόν
readings.en: it will rise at the end and not in vain
readings.plain: It will rise at the end, and not in vain

why: Mur88 preserves the Hebrew verb. The Greek seems to read yafi'a ("it will shine") for yafe'ach, and "not in vain" for "does not lie."

a: Even if it drags, wait for it
t: Wait for it, or wait for him?
p: The Greek makes the vision a person who might be late; Hebrews 10:37 follows it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves all these words
readings.en: if it delays, wait for it
readings.plain: Even if it drags, wait for it

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text); Hebrews 10:37
readings.en: if he is late, wait for him
readings.plain: If he is late, wait for him

why: The Hebrew "it" is the vision, grammatically feminine or neuter. The Greek "him" is a masculine, which lets "the coming one" be a person.
b: The Greek ends: "for the coming one will come and will not delay." Hebrews 10:37 uses that sentence with the article, "the One who is coming." The Hebrew ends: "for it will surely come; it will not delay."

a: Look, the one who is swollen with pride: the soul inside him is not upright
t: Swollen, or shrinking back?
p: The Hebrew describes a proud person; the Greek and Hebrews 10:38 have someone who shrinks back.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4Q82 (4QXII-g) preserves "swollen" and "upright"; Mur88 preserves "his soul in him" but restores "swollen"
readings.orig: הִנֵּה עֻפְּלָה לֹא יָשְׁרָה נַפְשׁוֹ בוֹ
readings.en: Look, swollen, not upright is his soul in him
readings.plain: Look, the one who is swollen with pride: the soul inside him is not upright

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text); Hebrews 10:38 (in the order of Hebrews)
readings.orig: ἐὰν ὑποστείληται, οὐκ εὐδοκεῖ ἡ ψυχή μου ἐν αὐτῷ
readings.en: if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him
readings.plain: If he shrinks back, my soul takes no pleasure in him

why: Two Hebrew scrolls (4Q82 and Mur88) support the Masoretic text for the words they preserve. The Greek may reflect a different Hebrew text or a free reading; the Hebrew is hard ('uppelah occurs once) but is not unreadable.
b: The two lines say nearly opposite things: the Hebrew condemns the proud; the Greek speaks of God's displeasure with a person who withdraws in fear. The Plain follows the Hebrew and gives the Greek in the variant; Hebrews 10:38 uses the Greek to call its readers to endure.

a: the righteous will live by his faithfulness
t: His faithfulness, my faithfulness, or faith?
p: Several forms of the line exist, and Paul's version has no pronoun at all.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); 4Q82 (4QXII-g) and Mur88 both read this word in full (printout); the Habakkuk Pesher (1QpHab), as published, quotes the verse with the same word in its lemma (not in this site's transcription data)
readings.en: and the righteous by his faithfulness will live
readings.plain: the righteous will live by his faithfulness

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text, which here agrees with Rahlfs's edition)
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεώς μου ζήσεται
readings.en: but the righteous will live by my faithfulness (God's)
readings.plain: the righteous will live by my faithfulness

readings.w: Hebrews 10:38; a few Septuagint manuscripts are reported to have "my" after "righteous" as well (Codex Alexandrinus is the one usually named), reported by commentators and not checked here
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ δίκαιός μου ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται
readings.en: but my righteous one will live by faith
readings.plain: my righteous one will live by faith

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome), as reported by commentators; not in this site's transcription data
readings.orig: iustus autem in fide sua vivet
readings.en: but the righteous will live in his faith
readings.plain: the righteous will live by his faith

readings.w: Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11 (Paul)
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ δίκαιος ἐκ πίστεως ζήσεται
readings.en: but the righteous will live by faith
readings.plain: the righteous will live by faith

why: The Hebrew is the base text, and two scrolls, 4Q82 and Mur88, read it as the Masoretic Text does, "by his faithfulness"; the pesher's quotation, as published, has the same word. The Plain follows it and notes that Paul's Greek drops both "his" and "my."
b: Where each reading goes. "His" in the Hebrew belongs to the righteous person. "My" in the Septuagint belongs to God, so the righteous live by God's faithfulness. Hebrews puts "my" on the righteous one. The Vulgate has "his faith," the form Luther and Jerome's readers knew. Paul omits the pronoun, which keeps the way open for readers to ask whose faith. The Qumran commentary quotes the line as "by his faithfulness" (be'emunato) in the lemma, but its comment reads 'emunatam, "their faithfulness," and explains it as faithfulness to the Teacher of Righteousness (see the note on the verse). Not checked here: the Greek scroll of the Twelve from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, a revision of the Greek toward the Hebrew, the kaige group), the later Greek revisions of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion, the Peshitta and the Targum are not in this site's data, and I do not state their wording; for them see the apparatus of the Göttingen Septuagint and the commentaries listed with the book. For the debate between churches about what Paul means by faith, see the card on this chapter.

a: wine is a traitor
t: Wine or wealth?
p: The Qumran commentary's quotation has "wealth"; the Hebrew has "wine."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 reads "the wine" in full
readings.plain: wine is a traitor

readings.w: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab), as published by Horgan and in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible; this site's transcription data does not include this scroll
readings.plain: wealth is a traitor

why: Mur88 preserves the Masoretic reading, which the Greek also seems to know. "Wealth" is close to "wine" in Hebrew letters (hon and yayin), and fits the commentary's application to a priest who betrayed for money.
b: The Greek has "the proud man is a scoffer," which reads the line very differently and uses "scoffer" again for the Hebrew boged.

a: pouring out your anger, and making them drunk as well
t: Your anger or his anger?
p: The Hebrew changes from "his neighbor" to "your anger"; the Qumran text smooths it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (no scroll preserves this verse in the printout)
readings.plain: pouring out your anger, and making them drunk as well

readings.w: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab), as published by Horgan and in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible; this site's transcription data does not include this scroll
readings.plain: pouring out his anger, and making them drunk as well

why: The harder reading is the one with the change of person, and the third-person form looks like smoothing. The Greek has a different line ("with a muddy upset").

a: so as to look at their nakedness
t: Their nakedness or their festivals?
p: The Qumran commentary's text has a Hebrew word for "feasts," and uses it for the Day of Atonement.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.plain: so as to look at their nakedness

readings.w: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab), as published by Horgan and in the Dead Sea Scrolls Bible; this site's transcription data does not include this scroll
readings.plain: so as to look at their festivals

why: "Nakedness" is the Hebrew text, and fits the shaming in the next verse. "Festivals" is a one-letter change that serves the commentary's story of the Wicked Priest pursuing the Teacher on the Day of Atonement.

a: show that you are uncircumcised
t: Uncircumcised, or stagger?
p: The Hebrew says "be uncircumcised" (exposed); the Greek, and the Qumran commentary as reported, have "stagger."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (no scroll in this site's printout preserves this verse)
readings.plain: show that you are uncircumcised

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: stagger and reel

readings.w: Pesher Habakkuk (1QpHab) column XI, as reported in translation handbooks and scholarly discussion (not in this site's transcription data; I have not seen the scroll or Horgan's page myself)
readings.plain: and stagger

why: "Uncircumcised" keeps the shaming of 2:15 and is the harder reading, so the Plain keeps the Masoretic Text. The case for "stagger" is real: it is the same letters in another order, and both the Greek and, as reported, the Qumran lemma have it, so it is not only the Greek translator's guess.
b: The Qumran commentary is reported to quote the verse with "and stagger" and then, in its comment, to speak of a priest who "did not circumcise the foreskin of his heart" (Vermes's translation), so its interpretation plays on both senses. I rely here on translation handbooks and scholarly discussion for the lemma, not on a reading of the scroll; the lemma is therefore labeled "as reported."

a: will terrify you
t: Terrify you, or terrify them?
p: The Masoretic word means "terrify them"; the Greek says "you."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex) (no scroll preserves this verse in the printout)
readings.plain: will terrify them

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: will terrify you

why: "Them" has nothing to refer to in the Hebrew. The Greek "you" fits the whole woe, which is addressed to "you." The Plain follows the Greek here, and again at 3:6, where the Greek sense requires a different pointing of the Hebrew verb.
b: Some commentators emend the Hebrew to yechitekha ("will terrify you"), a small change in the last letters, which would explain the Greek.

a: In the middle of the years make it known
t: The middle of the years, or two living things?
p: The Greek reads "in the midst of two living things," which later Christians linked to the manger.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves "in the midst of years" in full
readings.en: in the midst of years you will make known
readings.plain: In the middle of the years make it known

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text); the early Latin versions follow it
readings.en: in the midst of two living things you will be made known
readings.plain: In the middle of two living things you will be made known

why: Mur88 reads the Hebrew as the Masoretic Text does. The Greek seems to have read shanim ("years") as shenayim ("two") and chayyehu ("revive it") as chayyot or chayyim ("living things").
b: The Greek has a second form: "when the years draw near you will be known." Augustine (City of God 18.32, with 18.33) reads "two living things" as the two Testaments, as Christ between the two thieves, or as Moses and Elijah at the Transfiguration; later writers added the ox and the donkey at the manger. The Old Latin follows the Greek (in medio duorum animalium); Jerome's Vulgate has in medio annorum ("in the midst of the years"), as the Hebrew does. These are Christian readings of the Greek, not the Hebrew.

a: Rays shoot from his hand
t: Rays or horns?
p: The Hebrew has qarnayim, which means rays or horns; Hebrew and Greek agree on the word.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 restores the word
readings.en: horns/rays from his hand to him
readings.plain: Rays shoot from his hand

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: Horns are in his hands

why: Both witnesses read the same Hebrew word; the difference is how to translate it. In a verse about light, "rays" suits (compare the verb of Moses' shining face in Exodus 34).
b: The Leningrad Codex records a different spelling of the last word of the verse in its margin; the Dead Sea scroll Mur88 writes the ending with a final he, like the written form. This is spelling, not meaning.

a: Plague goes in front of him
t: Plague or word?
p: The Hebrew deber ("plague") and dabar ("word") have the same consonants; the Greek reads "word."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 reads the consonants in full
readings.plain: Plague goes in front of him

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: A word goes in front of him

why: Plague pairs with the next line's "fever" (resheph) and with Deuteronomy 32:24. The Greek vocalizes the same letters as dabar.

a: He stands, and the earth shakes
t: Does he shake the earth or measure it?
p: The same consonants can be read "measured" (Masoretic pointing, and the Latin) or "shook."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves the verb in full
readings.plain: He stands and measures the earth

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text) ("was shaken"); also the sense of many modern commentators
readings.plain: He stands, and the earth shakes

why: The Masoretic pointing reads "measured." The Plain follows the Greek sense, "shook" (a verb many commentators propose from a root mud, which would need a different pointing of the Hebrew), because the next lines have the nations jumping and the mountains breaking. This is a re-pointing proposed by commentators and supported by the Greek, not a different Hebrew text found in any witness.

a: your chariots of rescue
t: Chariots, or cavalry?
p: A spelling difference in Mur88 and a different word in the Greek.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 restores the first "rivers" but preserves the second, "the sea" and "horses"
readings.plain: your chariots of rescue

readings.w: Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (the printout marks the word as differing in spelling, with an added vowel letter)
readings.plain: your chariots of rescue

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: your cavalry is rescue

why: The Hebrew "chariots" matches the horses of the line before. Mur88's spelling is not a difference in meaning. The Greek has a general word for horsemanship.

a: Oaths are sworn on the arrows: a word.
t: The hardest line in the chapter
p: At least four readings; the Hebrew has "oaths, rods/arrows, a word."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves "oaths, rods/arrows, a word" and "Selah" in full
readings.plain: Oaths are sworn on the arrows: a word.

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome)
readings.en: the oaths you spoke to the tribes
readings.plain: Oaths to the tribes: a word.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.orig: ἐντείνων ἐνέτεινας τόξον σου ἐπὶ σκῆπτρα, λέγει Κύριος
readings.en: you stretch your bow over scepters, says the LORD
readings.plain: You stretch your bow over the scepters, says the LORD.

why: The Hebrew is the base text, and "arrows" is the closest to the printed word matot in this context. The Greek and Latin each show an old interpretation; none is certain.

a: A flood of water rushes past
t: "Passes over" or "thick"?
p: The Dead Sea scroll Mur88 has a different word in the last position.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: a downpour of water passed over
readings.plain: A flood of water rushes past

readings.w: Murabba'at scroll Mur88 (the printout marks this word as differing from the Masoretic text)
readings.plain: A flood of dense water

why: Mur88 has the letters '-b-w-t where the Masoretic Text has '-b-r; the scroll's reading is a real variant, and I do not propose how it arose. The Masoretic reading gives a clear verb, and "thick" would need an unusual phrase.
b: Mur88 also writes the first word of the line with a different spelling (zeramu), which is not a difference in meaning.

a: Sun and moon stand still in their lofty home
t: Did the sun stand still, or rise?
p: The Greek has the sun lifted and the moon standing in its place.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 has the same, with a different spelling of "lofty home"
readings.en: sun, moon stood still [in] their lofty abode
readings.plain: Sun and moon stand still in their lofty home

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.orig: ἐπήρθη ὁ ἥλιος, καὶ ἡ σελήνη ἔστη ἐν τῇ τάξει αὐτῆς
readings.en: the sun was lifted up, and the moon stood in its order
readings.plain: The sun is lifted up, and the moon stands in its place

why: Mur88 supports the Hebrew in all the words it preserves; its spelling zevulah with a vowel letter is a spelling difference. The Greek is freer.

a: to rescue your anointed one
t: To rescue the anointed, or to rescue with him?
p: The Hebrew word et can be the object marker or the word "with"; the Latin took the second.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves the word et
readings.en: for the rescue of [et] your anointed
readings.plain: to rescue your anointed one

readings.w: Latin Vulgate (Jerome)
readings.plain: to rescue with your anointed one

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.plain: to rescue your anointed one

why: The Hebrew object marker and the Greek agree, and "with" would be an odd use. The Vulgate's reading depends on a different understanding of 'et.

a: the head of his warriors
t: One warrior or many?
p: The Leningrad Codex writes one form and reads another; Mur88 writes the singular.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), reading (Qere)
readings.plain: the head of his warriors

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), writing (Ketiv); Mur88 reads the same letters
readings.plain: the head of his warrior

why: The singular is the written form and may be a collective; the plural is the one the Masoretes read. The meaning is about the same. The Plain follows the reading tradition.

a: even if the flock is cut off from the pen
t: Cut off from the pen, or short of food?
p: The Greek has "the sheep have run out of food."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves "cut off"
readings.en: the flock is cut off from the pen
readings.plain: even if the flock is cut off from the pen

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.en: the sheep have failed from food
readings.plain: even if the sheep run short of food

why: The Hebrew word mikhlah means a fold or pen (Psalm 50:9; Psalm 78:70); the Greek takes it as "food." The Hebrew is the more specific image.

a: He makes my feet like a doe's
t: Like a doe's, or to a finish?
p: The Greek reads a different word for "like does."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Mur88 preserves "like does"
readings.en: and he makes my feet like does
readings.plain: He makes my feet like a doe's

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation made before Jesus; Swete's text)
readings.orig: τάξει τοὺς πόδας μου εἰς συντέλειαν
readings.en: he will set my feet to a completion
readings.plain: He sets my feet toward the finish

why: The Hebrew is the same line as 2 Samuel 22:34 and Psalm 18:33. The Greek has misread ke'ayyalot as a word from kalah ("finish").
